Abstract.AbstractText: Perioperative visual loss (POVL) after spinal surgery is a devastating complication for both the patient and the surgical team. Two major causes are known: ischemic optic neuropathy (ION) and central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The traditional understanding of CRAO has been consistently related to the occurrence of periocular trauma and signs of increased intraorbital pressure in addition to visual loss. Such orbital signs are, however, not a feature of any common POVL syndrome. A 55-year-old woman underwent prolonged lumbar decompression and fusion for spinal stenosis under general anesthesia in the prone position. At the end of the surgery, some periocular hyperemia, corneal edema, and a tense orbit on the right side were noted. Complete internal and external ophthalmoplegia was observed on examination. Orbital computed tomography confirmed the clinical diagnosis of an orbital compartment syndrome (OCS). Bony decompression was performed, but the treated eye remained blind. Resolution of the complete ophthalmoplegia was observed in the late follow-up. In retrospect, patients diagnosed with the often-misunderstood CRAO and ION with orbital signs after spinal surgery most likely had OCS. The inclusion of orbital signs in the clinical picture of ION and CRAO is not only incorrect but gives the impression of therapeutic futility, thereby preventing successful orbital decompression in a timely fashion.
